topic: moving twenty-four beehives to a heather site and planning the late-season crop

provenance.author: subagent-en-a
provenance.notes: independent English scenario, not a translation; five sentences per turn

a: Here are six hive weights in kilograms: 38, 52, 41, 47, 33 and 56.
Sort those six numbers from the heaviest hive down to the lightest and keep them as whole numbers.
Give me the total weight of the six hives and the mean weight rounded to one decimal place.
Tell me which of them sit above forty-five kilograms and how many hives that is in all.
Then convert that total into metric tonnes and write the figure out with three decimal places.
base: We keep twenty-four colonies at the home apiary, and the heather opens on the moor in about three weeks.
The moor site is forty kilometres away, over a road that climbs steadily for the last ten.
I have never shifted this many colonies at once, and the weight of the full boxes worries me.
Several of the strongest hives are still heavy with summer honey that we have not taken off.
Before I fix a date, I want to know what is realistic with one van and one trailer.

a: Sorted from heaviest to lightest the six hives run 56, 52, 47, 41, 38 and 33 kilograms.
The six hives come to 267 kilograms in total, so the mean weight is 44.5 kilograms.
Three of them sit above forty-five kilograms, namely the hives of 56, 52 and 47 kilograms.
In metric tonnes the total is 0.267, written out to the three decimal places you wanted.
The other three hives together weigh 112 kilograms, which is the lighter half of the load.
base: Forty kilometres is short enough to run in the dark, and darkness is the part that matters.
Close the entrances after dusk, when every forager is home, and the colony travels as one unit.
The climb at the end is where the straps earn their keep, because braking shoves the boxes forward.
How are the hives made up, single brood boxes or doubles with supers still stacked on top?
That decides both the weight per hive and how much movement you have to hold still.

a: The trailer takes ten hives per trip and the van takes four hives on its own floor.
Work out how many full trips are needed to move twenty-four hives with both vehicles loaded.
One round trip to the moor and back is eighty kilometres, so give me the total distance.
Assume forty minutes of driving each way and twenty minutes of loading at either end.
Add that up and give me the total time in hours and minutes for the whole move.
base: They are single brood boxes with one super on most, and two supers on the four strongest.
The van will hold four hives on the floor, and the trailer takes ten if I strap them well.
That means more than one trip, and I am not sure whether to split the apiary in half.
Would it be better to take the heavy ones first while the night is still cool?
The far end of the road has no lights and I would rather not be there at dawn.

a: Two trips are enough, because the van and the trailer carry fourteen hives together each time.
The first trip moves fourteen hives, and the second moves the remaining ten hives.
Two round trips of eighty kilometres each give a total distance of one hundred and sixty kilometres.
Each trip costs two hours, made up of eighty minutes driving and forty minutes loading.
The whole move therefore takes four hours, counting driving and handling from first strap to last.
base: Taking the heavy ones first is right, because the cool part of the night is the safe part.
Strap each hive as a single block, floor to roof, and run the ratchet over the top.
Leave the mesh floors open so the cluster can shed heat while the boxes are shut.
Do not split the apiary across two nights unless you have to, since the field bees drift.
One night, two trips, everything home before first light is the shape to aim for.

a: Here is the kit list: ratchet straps, mesh travel screens, entrance blocks, smoker, hive tool and spare boxes.
Split that list into things needed during loading and things needed only at the moor site.
Write each group out as a plain list, in the same order the items appear above.
Then count the items in each group and give me the two totals side by side.
Keep the smoker in the loading group and make sure nothing appears in both groups.
base: The mesh floors are open on every hive, so heat should not be the worst of it.
What I am less sure about is the site itself, which I only walked once in June.
There is a track to within thirty metres of the stand, then heather and soft ground.
Water is a burn about two hundred metres down the slope, and the stand faces west.
I would rather set the hives out properly than shuffle them a week later.

a: The loading group holds the ratchet straps, the mesh travel screens, the entrance blocks and the smoker.
The moor group holds the hive tool and the spare boxes, in the order they were given.
That makes four items in the loading group and two items in the moor group.
The smoker stays in the loading group, exactly as instructed, and appears nowhere else.
No item has been listed twice, and the original order has been kept inside each group.
base: West facing is good on the moor, because the stand warms early and dries after mist.
Thirty metres of soft ground is the real cost, since every full box is carried by hand.
Set the hives in pairs with the entrances quartered, so the returning bees sort themselves out.
Keep them off the wet with pallets or blocks, and leave a clear lane behind the row.
The burn is far enough that they will find nearer damp ground in the heather anyway.

a: Now take the twelve stands at the moor site and number them from one through to twelve.
Assign the fourteen hives from the first trip to those stands, at two hives per stand.
Fill the stands in order and tell me the highest stand number that gets used.
Then say how many stands are still standing empty once the first trip is unloaded.
Give me the result as three short lines and leave out any extra commentary.
base: How long should I leave them on the heather before I think about bringing them back?
The flow here usually runs three weeks, though last year the wind flattened the last of it.
I also need to decide when the crop comes off, on the moor or back at home.
Heather honey does not run out of the comb, so pressing or loosening is a job in itself.
And the colonies still have to be fed and treated before winter closes in.

a: Stands one through to seven each take two hives, which uses all fourteen hives exactly.
The highest stand number that gets used on the first trip is therefore stand seven.
Stands eight through to twelve stay empty, which leaves five empty stands after the first trip.
No stand carries a single hive, because fourteen divides evenly into pairs across seven stands.
Those are the three lines: seven stands filled, highest stand seven, and five stands empty.
base: Three weeks on the heather is the normal run, and the wind decides the last week.
Bring them home when the bell heather browns off and the bees start working the edges.
Take the crop off at home, where you have room and a warm place to press.
Heather honey is thixotropic, so it has to be stirred or pricked before it will leave the comb.
Feed straight after extraction and treat before the cluster tightens for the cold.

a: Write out the loading steps in order, starting with closing the entrances and finishing with the straps.
Number the steps from one to six and keep each step to a single short line.
Use exactly the same wording for the second trip and mark which of the steps are repeated.
Then list the unloading steps at the moor site in the order they actually happen.
Keep both lists plain and do not add any explanation in between the steps.
base: That helps a lot, though the pressing is the part I have never done at scale.
I have a small press and about forty frames of heather likely to come back.
The rest of the crop is ordinary summer honey that will spin off without trouble.
I would rather not mix the two, since the heather is worth far more by the jar.
Is there a sensible order to work through the boxes when they come off the trailer?

a: Loading runs: close entrances, fit travel screens, strap each hive, load the trailer, load the van, check straps.
The second trip repeats steps one through six with the ten remaining hives, in the same order.
Steps three, four and five are the ones repeated with different boxes on the second run.
Unloading runs: unstrap, carry to stand, set level, remove travel screen, open entrance, move on.
Both lists are set out plain, with no explanation added in between the numbered steps.
base: Work the boxes in the order they come off, and keep the heather supers to one side.
Anything with a hard, jelly-like feel in the cells is heather and should not go near the spinner.
Press those frames in small batches while the wax is still warm from the drive home.
Spin the ordinary supers first, since they clear quickly and free the room for pressing.
Label the two crops as they are jarred, because they are impossible to tell apart cold.
